html:
In 186 BCE the Roman Senate cracked down on the Bacchanalia, the secret rites of the wine god Bacchus, known to the Greeks as Dionysus. Thousands were accused and many were executed. It was the first large religious persecution in Roman history.

The cult had spread up from southern Italy and Etruria and drew men and women, free and slave, to night meetings. According to Livy, a young man named Aebutius and his lover, the freedwoman Hispala, told the consul that the meetings hid crimes, from sexual abuse to forgery and murder. The Senate treated it as a conspiracy against the state. Livy says about seven thousand people were involved.

The Senate did not ban the god. It put the cult under state control: no Bacchic group could meet without permission, gatherings were limited to five people, no man could be a priest, and members could not share a common fund. A bronze copy of the decree was found in 1640 in Calabria. Rome welcomed foreign gods, as with the Great Mother, but only on its own terms, a pattern later seen with Christianity.
